claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy containing Cu, Ni, other co-alloying elements, and minimal Pd/Pt.
Mild chemical or electrochemical dealloying can selectively remove Ni or other less noble elements from the catalyst.
Selective removal of Ni will enrich the catalyst surface in Cu.
Minimal Pd/Pt will be retained and remain well dispersed after dealloying.
Dealloying will restructure the surface into Cu-enriched nanoparticulate clusters.
The restructured surface will form robust oxide interfaces.
The oxide interfaces will resist catalyst sintering.
The restructured surface and oxide interfaces will resist poisoning.
Selective dealloying removes elements that are less catalytically beneficial.
Cu and retained minimal Pd/Pt enrichment creates stable catalytic sites.
The stable sites lower the oxidation onset temperature.
The stable sites improve resistance to H2O and NO poisoning.
The stable sites enhance durability during thermal cycling.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, dealloying will lower the light-off temperature for CO oxidation.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, dealloying will lower the light-off temperature for hydrocarbon oxidation.
The dealloyed catalyst will sustain greater activity in the presence of H2O and NO than the untreated catalyst.
The dealloyed catalyst will undergo less structural degradation or sintering after accelerated aging than the untreated catalyst.
The proposed benefits should apply under transient exhaust containing H2O, NO, CO, and hydrocarbons at approximately 100–150 °C.
The proposed benefits are anticipated across typical automotive exhaust conditions at approximately 100–300 °C.
Very high temperatures or non-standard exhaust mixtures may not produce the same improvements.
